answer:
The fastest air-breathing manned aircraft is the **Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird**, which holds the world record for the fastest speed achieved by a manned, air-breathing jet-powered aircraft. It reached speeds exceeding **Mach 3.3** (approximately 2,200 mph or 3,540 km/h).

The SR-71 Blackbird was **mostly made of titanium**. According to its design specifications:
*   Approximately **85% of the airframe's structure** was constructed from titanium alloys.
*   The remaining **~15%** was made of polymer composite materials.

Titanium was chosen because it has an exceptionally low coefficient of thermal expansion compared to most other metals. When the SR-71 flew at Mach 3+, the friction of the air caused the entire aircraft skin to heat up to approximately **600°F (315°C)**. Most metals would warp or deform at these temperatures, but titanium expanded predictably and remained strong enough to handle the extreme stress. In fact, when the plane was sitting on the ground "cool," the panels were loosely fitted so that as they expanded during flight, everything fit snugly together.

### Designation as SR-71
During the 1964 campaign, Republican presidential nominee Barry Goldwater repeatedly criticized President Lyndon B. Johnson and his administration for falling behind the Soviet Union in developing new weapons. Johnson decided to counter this criticism by revealing the existence of the YF-12A USAF interceptor, which also served as cover for the still-secret A-12[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-oxcartstory-27) and the USAF reconnaissance model since July 1964. USAF Chief of Staff General Curtis LeMay preferred the SR (Strategic Reconnaissance) designation and wanted the RS-71 to be named SR-71. Before the July speech, LeMay lobbied to modify Johnson's speech to read "SR-71" instead of "RS-71". The media transcript given to the press at the time still had the earlier RS-71 designation in places, creating the story that the president had misread the aircraft's designation.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-28)[[N 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-29) To conceal the A-12's existence, Johnson referred only to the A-11, while revealing the existence of a high-speed, high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-30)
In 1968, Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara canceled the F-12 interceptor program. The specialized tooling used to manufacture both the YF-12 and the SR-71 was also ordered destroyed.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-Landis_p47-31) Production of the SR-71 totaled 32 aircraft: 29 SR-71As, 2 SR-71Bs, and 1 SR-71C.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-32)
Tandem cockpits
Interior of pilot's cockpit

### Designation as SR-71
No-step areas are outlined in red on the SR-71A at the Museum of Aviation, Robins AFB. Operational aircraft had the words NO STEP to indicate to which side of the line the warning applied.
The SR-71 was designed to fly faster than Mach3 at altitudes above 85,000 ft (26,000 m) with the smallest radar cross-section that Lockheed could achieve, an early attempt at stealth design.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrickmore200930%E2%80%9331-33) Aircraft were painted black to radiate heat more effectively than bare metal, reducing the temperature of the skin and thermal stresses on the airframe.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMerlin200916-34) It had tandem cockpits for its crew of two: a pilot and a reconnaissance systems officer who navigated and operated the surveillance systems.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham20086-35)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-crown-36)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham1996-37)

### Airframe, canopy, and landing gear
[edit]
Titanium was used for 85% of the structure, with much of the rest being polymercomposite materials.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-38) To control costs, Lockheed used a more easily worked titanium alloy, which softened at a lower temperature.[[N 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-42) The challenges posed led Lockheed to develop new fabrication methods, which have since been used in the manufacture of other aircraft. Lockheed found that washing welded titanium requires distilled water, as the chlorine present in tap water is corrosive; cadmium-plated tools could not be used, as they also caused corrosion.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-43) Metallurgical contamination was another problem; at one point, 80% of the delivered titanium for manufacture was rejected on these grounds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-44)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-45)
The high temperatures generated in flight required special design and operating techniques. Major sections of the skin of the inboard wings were corrugated, not smooth.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-46)

### Airframe, canopy, and landing gear
Fuselage panels were manufactured to fit only loosely with the aircraft on the ground. Proper alignment was achieved as the airframe heated up, with thermal expansion of several inches.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham199647-47) Because of this, and the lack of a fuel-sealing system that could remain leak-free with the extreme temperature cycles during flight, the aircraft leaked JP-7 fuel on the ground before takeoff,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham1996160-48) annoying ground crews.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-iwm20211103-26)
The outer windscreen of the cockpit was made of three layers of glass with cooling sections between them._[citation needed_] The ANS navigation window was made of solid quartz and was fused ultrasonically to the titanium frame.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-49) The temperature of the exterior of the windscreen could reach 600°F (320°C) during a mission.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham199641-50)
The Blackbird's tires, manufactured by B.F. Goodrich, contained aluminum and were inflated with nitrogen. They cost $2,300 each and generally required replacing within 20 missions. The Blackbird landed at more than 170 knots (200 mph; 310 km/h) and deployed a drag parachute to reduce landing roll and brake and tire wear.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-51)

It was capable of flying over Mach 3.2, roughly 2430 miles per hour, which is over three times faster than the speed of sound. While flying over Russian air space, if a ground-to-air missile threat was detected, the SR-71 could simply outrun the missile as their way of evasive action. This plane was the first attempt at a “stealth” plane through the exterior design, minimizing its radar cross-section. The dark blue paint helped increase the emission of internal heat and also provided camouflage in the night sky.

The empty weight of the SR-71 Blackbird was 59,000 lbs.

All metal expands when heated, it is a part of the chemical property. Titanium, unlike most metals out there, expands relatively little, making it the best option for the SR-71 Blackbird. Lockheed knew this when it designed the plane and specifically designed the aircraft to fit together better when in flight. When the plane was sitting on the ground before a flight, it was “cool” and the parts fit loosely into one another. It wouldn’t be until the plane was in flight and “heated” up that everything fit snuggly into each other. The large, “cool” surfaces on the aircraft had a corrugated texture that allowed the metal to expand as it heated up.
The plane’s ability to fly so fast was due to the state-of-the-art engines and the light weight nature of the aircraft. Ironically, the plane did not have enough thrust to get itself off the ground and into flight with full tanks of gas. After take-off, the SR-71 would almost immediately meet up with a fueling jet.

As a result, even the SR-71 would be easy prey for modern air defense systems like the S-400. As a result, major advances aircraft technology needed to occur before high-speed reconnaissance aircraft would again be survivable.

During the 1964 campaign, Republican presidential nominee Barry Goldwater repeatedly criticized President Lyndon B. Johnson and his administration for falling behind the Soviet Union in developing new weapons. Johnson decided to counter this criticism by revealing the existence of the YF-12A USAF interceptor, which also served as cover for the still-secret A-12[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-oxcartstory-27) and the USAF reconnaissance model since July 1964. USAF Chief of Staff General Curtis LeMay preferred the SR (Strategic Reconnaissance) designation and wanted the RS-71 to be named SR-71. Before the July speech, LeMay lobbied to modify Johnson's speech to read "SR-71" instead of "RS-71". Titanium was used for 85% of the structure, with much of the rest being polymercomposite materials.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-38) To control costs, Lockheed used a more easily worked titanium alloy, which softened at a lower temperature.[[N 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-42) The challenges posed led Lockheed to develop new fabrication methods, which have since been used in the manufacture of other aircraft. Since 1976, the Blackbird still holds the world record for the fastest “air-breathing manned aircraft.”
The SR-71 Blackbird, which got its name from the dark blue, almost black paint, was designed to fly over Mach 3 with a crew of two individuals; one pilot and one Reconnaissance Systems Officer. This plane was the first attempt at a “stealth” plane through the exterior design, minimizing its radar cross-section. The dark blue paint helped increase the emission of internal heat and also provided camouflage in the night sky.

When the plane was sitting on the ground before a flight, it was “cool” and the parts fit loosely into one another. Before the July speech, LeMay lobbied to modify Johnson's speech to read "SR-71" instead of "RS-71". The media transcript given to the press at the time still had the earlier RS-71 designation in places, creating the story that the president had misread the aircraft's designation.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-28)[[N 3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-29) To conceal the A-12's existence, Johnson referred only to the A-11, while revealing the existence of a high-speed, high-altitude reconnaissance aircraft.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-30)
In 1968, Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara canceled the F-12 interceptor program. The specialized tooling used to manufacture both the YF-12 and the SR-71 was also ordered destroyed.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-Landis_p47-31) Production of the SR-71 totaled 32 aircraft: 29 SR-71As, 2 SR-71Bs, and 1 SR-71C.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-32)

The SR-71 was designed to fly faster than Mach3 at altitudes above 85,000 ft (26,000 m) with the smallest radar cross-section that Lockheed could achieve, an early attempt at stealth design.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrickmore200930%E2%80%9331-33) Aircraft were painted black to radiate heat more effectively than bare metal, reducing the temperature of the skin and thermal stresses on the airframe.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMerlin200916-34) It had tandem cockpits for its crew of two: a pilot and a reconnaissance systems officer who navigated and operated the surveillance systems.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham20086-35)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-crown-36)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham1996-37)

Titanium was used for 85% of the structure, with much of the rest being polymercomposite materials.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-38) To control costs, Lockheed used a more easily worked titanium alloy, which softened at a lower temperature.[[N 4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-42) The challenges posed led Lockheed to develop new fabrication methods, which have since been used in the manufacture of other aircraft. Lockheed found that washing welded titanium requires distilled water, as the chlorine present in tap water is corrosive; cadmium-plated tools could not be used, as they also caused corrosion.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-43) Metallurgical contamination was another problem; at one point, 80% of the delivered titanium for manufacture was rejected on these grounds.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-44)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-45)
The high temperatures generated in flight required special design and operating techniques. Major sections of the skin of the inboard wings were corrugated, not smooth.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-46)

Fuselage panels were manufactured to fit only loosely with the aircraft on the ground. Proper alignment was achieved as the airframe heated up, with thermal expansion of several inches.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham199647-47) Because of this, and the lack of a fuel-sealing system that could remain leak-free with the extreme temperature cycles during flight, the aircraft leaked JP-7 fuel on the ground before takeoff,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham1996160-48) annoying ground crews.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-iwm20211103-26)
The outer windscreen of the cockpit was made of three layers of glass with cooling sections between them._[citation needed_] The ANS navigation window was made of solid quartz and was fused ultrasonically to the titanium frame.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-49) The temperature of the exterior of the windscreen could reach 600°F (320°C) during a mission.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGraham199641-50)
The Blackbird's tires, manufactured by B.F. Goodrich, contained aluminum and were inflated with nitrogen. They cost $2,300 each and generally required replacing within 20 missions. The Blackbird landed at more than 170 knots (200 mph; 310 km/h) and deployed a drag parachute to reduce landing roll and brake and tire wear.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_SR-71_Blackbird#cite_note-51)

The fastest air-breathing manned aircraft is the **Lockheed SR-71 Blackbird**, which holds the world record for the fastest speed achieved by a manned, air-breathing jet-powered aircraft. It reached speeds exceeding **Mach 3.3** (approximately 2,200 mph or 3,540 km/h).

The SR-71 Blackbird was **mostly made of titanium**. According to its design specifications:
*   Approximately **85% of the airframe's structure** was constructed from titanium alloys.
*   The remaining **~15%** was made of polymer composite materials.

Titanium was chosen because it has an exceptionally low coefficient of thermal expansion compared to most other metals. When the SR-71 flew at Mach 3+, the friction of the air caused the entire aircraft skin to heat up to approximately **600°F (315°C)**. Most metals would warp or deform at these temperatures, but titanium expanded predictably and remained strong enough to handle the extreme stress. In fact, when the plane was sitting on the ground "cool," the panels were loosely fitted so that as they expanded during flight, everything fit snugly together.
